analysis.one_liner: Sets a national floor of union organizing and bargaining rights for state and local government employees.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 34 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats and independents, but the Senate labor committee never acted on it and it died without a vote when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Private-sector workers have had a federal right to form unions and bargain since the 1930s. State and local government employees—teachers, public hospital nurses, transit workers, first responders—have no such federal right, and many states give them little or none. This bill would have the Federal Labor Relations Authority check each state's law, and in states that fall short of a federal floor, set nationwide bargaining standards covering union elections, employer recognition, written contracts, and grievance arbitration. States with comparable or stronger laws would be left alone.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local government employees in states where they currently lack full bargaining rights, plus labor unions that would gain members and a payroll-deduction channel for dues in those states.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public workers in states without bargaining rights

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Federal Labor Relations Authority to determine, within 180 days, whether each state's law substantially provides public employees the right to organize, join a union, and bargain collectively, and states falling short become subject to federal standards.

Where a state falls short, the federal standards require employers to recognize a union chosen by a majority vote, bargain in good faith over wages, hours, and working conditions, put any agreement in writing, resolve grievances through binding arbitration, and allow payroll deduction of union fees.

States with laws comparable to or stronger than the federal floor keep their own systems; the bill does not preempt stronger state or local rules, and exempts small towns (under 5,000 people or fewer than 25 public employees) that a state chooses to exclude.
The bill prohibits strikes, lockouts, and other job actions by emergency services employees and law enforcement officers when the result would measurably disrupt emergency or public safety services.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, and ultimately their taxpayers, who would face federally required bargaining, written contracts, and binding grievance arbitration where they do not already provide it.

drawbacks.text: The bill would override state law on public-sector labor relations in states that fall short of the federal floor, raising a federalism objection: labor law for state and local government workers has historically been a state matter, and the bill's justification rests on a contested reading of Congress's commerce power over state employment.

Requiring bargaining, written contracts, and binding arbitration imposes direct costs on state and local government budgets, which are funded by taxpayers, and the bill authorizes appropriations without a funding cap.

Defining which state laws 'substantially provide' the required rights leaves significant discretion to the Federal Labor Relations Authority, inviting prolonged litigation over each state's determination, with judicial review available to aggrieved employers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly half of states that provide little or no collective bargaining to public employees, the bill would deliver a real federal right to organize and bargain, with protections for governments that already do better and a strike ban for first responders to blunt the main public-safety objection. The main honest cost is fiscal—more bargaining and binding arbitration raises government labor costs, which fall on state and local taxpayers—and the main honest risk is a sweeping federal preemption of state labor policy under a contested legal theory.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2018 and referred to the Senate's labor committee, which never scheduled action on it, and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Mazie Hirono introduced the bill on June 27, 2018, with a list of Democratic and independent senators including the minority and whip leadership reading it into the record.
Thirty-four senators signed on as cosponsors, all Democrats plus one independent; no Republican did.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction; no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments in states with weak public-sector bargaining laws are better off, since no federal bargaining mandate ever took effect; public workers in those states gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State and local governments that escaped mandates

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors were Democrats plus one independent, and no Republican sponsor or cosponsor appears anywhere in the bill's history.

industries.note: A federal bargaining floor would let unions organize government workers in states that currently restrict it, and the bill specifically provides for payroll deduction of union fees in those states. Union gains run alongside workers' gains, since the same rules secure workers' bargaining rights.

Governments in states without full bargaining rights would face federally mandated union recognition, good-faith bargaining, written contracts, and binding grievance arbitration, with costs borne by their budgets and taxpayers. Their interest in avoiding the mandate runs directly against the workers the bill covers.
